content: In national censuses and decentralized monitoring systems, data collection is conducted to gather information on sanitation and hygiene. Household surveys, often led by national statistical authorities or supported externally through initiatives like the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) and the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), are typically conducted every four to five years. These surveys provide data at national and sometimes sub-national levels but often lack the granularity required for detailed local planning. Environmental health staff should be actively involved in training enumerators for these surveys to ensure the data collected is accurate, consistent, and aligned with established standards and targets. Providing surveyors with support tools, such as visual aids to classify technologies as improved or unimproved, can enhance data consistency. At the individual, utility, or sub-national monitoring level, environmental health officers may conduct monitoring activities and assist local authorities and health workers in tracking sanitation and hygiene behaviors. They should also monitor the containment, conveyance, treatment, and safe disposal or reuse of waste. When lapses are identified, corrective actions should be initiated with the responsible individuals or institutions. Given practical constraints, only a limited number of indicators can be monitored. Risk assessments should identify critical control points that require regular monitoring. At the global level, sanitation is tracked using the indicator of the proportion of the population utilizing safely managed sanitation services. This is defined as the use of improved sanitation facilities that are not shared with other households, where excreta are either treated and disposed of in situ, stored temporarily and transported to off-site treatment, or transported via sewer systems with wastewater for off-site treatment. National monitoring systems should include core indicators that align with global monitoring elements while also capturing additional nationally relevant aspects of safe management and implementation. Environmental health officers play a crucial role in collecting data on sanitation facilities, their usage, and related behaviors. This includes assessing the safety and effectiveness of on-site treatment, the emptying and transport of fecal sludge, the extent of untreated sewage leakage or overflow, and the compliance of sludge and sewage treatment with national standards. Community engagement on sanitation should also be evaluated. Data collection on sanitation and handwashing facilities, as well as on-site treatment, should involve inspections of dwellings and buildings, either routinely, during special surveys, or as part of national censuses. Information on the emptying and transport of on-site facilities and untreated sewage leakage should be gathered from customers, operators, and regulatory bodies. Data on the effectiveness of sludge and sewage treatment should be collected from operators and verified through independent sampling and laboratory analysis. Service providers should report specified monitoring information, subject to inspection by environmental health authorities. The frequency of inspections depends on the level of trust in service providers and the potential hazards of non-compliance. Information on community engagement in sanitation requires discussions with local officials and community members. Comprehensive sanitary inspection forms have been developed to assist environmental health officers in this process. Monitoring systems should ideally maintain a georeferenced database of sanitation facilities and their conditions to aid in planning and managing interventions. This database can also inform the design of sanitation promotion strategies. Sanitation services must be tailored to the physical, social, and economic conditions of each area, with assessments conducted to identify inadequacies in the existing sanitation situation. This process should involve stakeholders to develop a shared understanding of the issues and formulate feasible solutions that address public health risks. Sanitation solutions should encompass hardware, promotion and behavior change, institutional development, legislation and regulation, and financing. Wherever possible, existing capacity and infrastructure should be utilized. Sanitation services may be provided by the private sector, utility companies, local governments, or a combination of these. Poorer households should have access to subsidies to ensure affordability. Major capital investments, such as for fecal sludge treatment and sewerage systems, often require public funding and may be managed by public entities, utility companies, or private operators. Decentralized sanitation systems, including small sewerage systems and fecal sludge transfer facilities, are increasingly necessary in urban areas. These systems may face challenges such as land acquisition or community resistance, which can often be addressed through community engagement and incentives. Treatment technologies like anaerobic baffled reactors or upflow anaerobic sludge blankets can be installed underground, creating community spaces and generating biogas for local use. Capacity building for sanitation services requires partnerships with academic institutions, NGOs, or social enterprises to support technical development and adaptation. Franchise models can be considered for mature services, providing training, technical support, quality control, and marketing. Partnerships should include environmental health experts to oversee risk assessments, system improvements, and operational monitoring. Associations of service providers can facilitate dialogue with authorities, support training and certification, and help develop credit lines for sanitation businesses. Training and peer-to-peer learning are essential components of capacity building.
